           Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure1 and

the Commission’s Notice of Extension of Time of August 25, 2026, intervenor North

Carolina Electric Membership Corporation (“NCEMC”)2 protests the application

submitted by NextEra Energy, Inc., (“NextEra”) and Dominion Energy, Inc.,

(“Dominion”) on behalf of themselves and their Commission-jurisdictional holding-

company and public-utility subsidiaries (together, the “Applicants”), for a Commission

order under sections 203(a)(1) and (2) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”)3 authorizing the

proposed merger of NextEra and Dominion.4

 I.         Introduction

           The Commission may authorize the proposed merger only if it finds the merger

“will be consistent with the public interest,”5 and it may impose terms and conditions that

it finds “necessary or appropriate” to secure the public interest.6

           The Applicants have submitted what can only be described as a bare-bones

application.7 The commitments and conditions proposed by the Applicants are manifestly

inadequate to ensure the proposed merger is consistent with the public interest,

particularly given that (1) Applicants have seen the need to commit to reduce certain

Virginia retail customers’ bills by $10/month for four years to ensure the proposed

merger is consistent with the public interest8 but (2) Applicants have made no similar

commitment to help mitigate the increased bills that will be received by North Carolina’s

rural cooperative end-use consumers whose bills are materially impacted by Dominion’s

wholesale transmission rates.

        NCEMC delivers power to serve its member distribution cooperatives’ systems in

northeastern North Carolina over transmission facilities operated by the PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), and owned by Dominion’s public-utility subsidiary,

Virginia Electric and Power Company (“VEPCO”). NCEMC’s primary concern in this

proceeding is how the proposed merger may affect VEPCO’s transmission rates,

transmission incentives, and transmission-investment decisions that ultimately determine

the costs borne by NCEMC’s members and their consumers. The conditions requested in

this Protest aim to protect rural North Carolina consumers from the adverse transmission-

related effects of the proposed merger.

       In particular, NCEMC requests, in addition to other appropriate consumer relief

found by the Commission to be in the public interest, that the Commission authorize the

proposed merger only on the following additional necessary and appropriate conditions:

              That VEPCO amend its transmission formula rate by removing the 50-
               basis-point “RTO Adder” for its membership in PJM.
              That the Applicants establish and fund an Independent Transmission
               Monitor for an initial five-year term, subject to Commission review at the
               conclusion of that period.
              That VEPCO amend its transmission formula rate by adding terms and
               conditions to ensure the effectiveness and enforceability of the Applicants’
               hold-harmless commitment to transmission customers and the Applicants’
               public Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
              That the Commission impose on the Applicants additional restrictions on
               affiliate transactions to prevent the merged company’s transmission
               customers from cross-subsidizing affiliated companies.
              That VEPCO amend its transmission formula rate by reforming the
               blanket 50% hold back of revenue credits for secondary uses of
               transmission facilities.
       NCEMC further explains the basis for these conditions in Parts II.A–II.E below.




                                            3
         A.       NCEMC and its interest in this proceeding

        NCEMC is a generation and transmission cooperative responsible for the full or

partial power supply requirements of its 25 members throughout the state of North

Carolina. Those 25 distribution cooperatives, in turn, supply electricity to approximately

one million homes, farms, and businesses in which more than 2.8 million North

Carolinians live and work.

        NCEMC serves distribution-cooperative loads located throughout the service

areas of three investor-owned public utilities: Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, and Duke

Energy Progress, LLC, both subsidiaries of Duke Energy Corporation (“Duke”), and

VEPCO, doing business as Dominion Energy Virginia in Virginia and as Dominion

Energy North Carolina in North Carolina.

        NCEMC is a member of PJM, a member of PJM’s Electric Distributor sector, a

PJM load-serving entity, a PJM transmission customer, and a participant in PJM’s

energy, ancillary services, capacity, and financial transmission rights markets.

        PJM operates transmission facilities owned by VEPCO and other electric utilities.

NCEMC purchases transmission services from PJM over VEPCO’s transmission

facilities to serve the loads of its six member cooperatives that distribute power at retail

in the Dominion Zone of the PJM region. NCEMC pays PJM for transmission services at

rates that are determined in large part by the transmission revenue requirement

established by VEPCO’s transmission formula rate in the PJM Open Access

Transmission Tariff.9

         VEPCO’s transmission rate is substantially higher than those paid by NCEMC for

its members served through the Duke transmission systems. Based on current projections,

VEPCO’s 2026 transmission rate is approximately three times comparable Duke

transmission rates on a $/MW-month basis, and it is expected to remain materially higher

given the concentration of large-load growth in Northern Virginia and the substantial

transmission investment planned to serve that growth. Recent VEPCO projections

indicate a 2027 transmission rate of approximately $8,269/MW-month, reflecting, among

other factors, a more than $2.4 billion increase in transmission plant in service and only a

modest increase in the transmission-rate divisor.10

        The primary driver of the increase in the transmission rate is the continued growth

in VEPCO’s transmission plant balances, which are projected to increase by billions of

dollars annually. Although demand growth in the Dominion Zone is substantial, projected

increases in transmission plant significantly outpace growth in the coincident peak

demand used to allocate transmission costs. As a result, transmission rates are projected

to continue increasing notwithstanding growth in the transmission-rate divisor. These

increasing rates translate into higher bundled bills for end-of-the-line rural cooperative

consumers. As a VEPCO transmission customer and power supplier to Northeastern

North Carolina’s cooperatives, NCEMC has a direct and substantial interest in ensuring

that VEPCO’s transmission rates remain just and reasonable and that its transmission

investments are subject to appropriate oversight and accountability.

        These concerns directly inform the merger-related issues raised in this Protest,

including elimination of the RTO Adder in VEPCO’s transmission formula rate;

establishment of an Independent Transmission Monitor for matters affecting the

Dominion Zone and PJM planning processes involving Dominion and NextEra affiliates;

establishment of clear restrictions on VEPCO transactions with its many new corporate

affiliates; and reformation of the revenue-sharing allocation for secondary use of

VEPCO’s transmission system. Elimination of the RTO Adder would provide meaningful

near-term transmission-rate relief to NCEMC and its member cooperatives, as well as

other customers throughout North Carolina. In addition, given the growing disparity

between VEPCO and Duke transmission rates and the substantial transmission

investment anticipated in the Dominion Zone, enhanced independent oversight of

transmission planning, project development, and cost recovery is warranted. An

Independent Transmission Monitor would help ensure that transmission investments are

appropriately justified, efficiently designed, and supported by demonstrable customer

benefits while providing greater transparency regarding future rate impacts, project costs,

and transmission-related cost recovery. Establishing clear restrictions on affiliate

transactions between VEPCO and the merged company’s many affiliated companies is

essential to protecting VEPCO transmission customers from inappropriate cross-

subsidization of these affiliates and the merged company’s shareholders. Likewise,

reformation of the revenue-sharing mechanism in VEPCO’s transmission formula rate

would also prevent cross-subsidization and provide meaningful rate relief to NCEMC and

its member cooperatives, as well as other transmission consumers.




                                              6
            While Applicants have committed to protect customers from merger-related costs,

they have not proposed meaningful relief from the underlying transmission-rate pressures

driving costs for VEPCO transmission customers.11 The distinction is important. The

Applicants’ hold-harmless commitment prevents customers from bearing costs related to

the transaction itself; it does not protect customers from continued growth in transmission

rates resulting from increased transmission investment or from continued recovery of

transmission incentives that no longer serve their intended purpose. The Applicants’

verification that the proposed transaction itself will not result in an improper cross-

subsidization of a non-utility associate company or a pledge or encumbrance of utility

assets12 does not protect against increased monetization of secondary uses of the

transmissions system for the benefit of shareholders of the new, larger combined

company, or cross-subsidization through affiliate transactions within the byzantine

structure of the merged company.

           Importantly, although Applicants have emphasized substantial customer benefits

in support of the proposed merger, including billions of dollars of bill credits for certain

of the Applicants’ retail customers, they have not proposed any comparable mechanism

to provide rate relief for wholesale transmission customers—like NCEMC and its

members—whose costs are directly affected by VEPCO’s transmission rates.13

            Accordingly, NCEMC’s requested conditions are directed not merely at merger

costs, but at the proposed merger’s broader effects on transmission rates that the

Commission must evaluate in its analysis of the public interest under FPA section 203.

Indeed, the Commission Staff recently confirmed the relevance of these broader concerns

in a deficiency letter issued in this proceeding, requesting that Applicants identify

Dominion public-utility subsidiaries serving customers under cost-based rates, including

wholesale transmission customers, and explain how the proposed transaction will affect

those rates, “particularly as to cost components other than any potential transaction-

related costs.”14 The Commission’s inquiry underscores that a hold-harmless commitment

addressing transaction and transition costs does not, by itself, resolve the rate-effects

inquiry required under section 203.

           B.       The Commission has broad authority under section 203 of the Federal
                    Power Act to protect the public interest when it considers merger
                    applications.

           Under section 203(a)(4) of the FPA, the Commission may authorize a proposed

utility merger “if it finds that the proposed transaction will be consistent with the public

interest.”15 In addition, the Commission must find that the proposed merger “will not

result in cross-subsidization of a non-utility associate company or the pledge or

encumbrance of utility assets for the benefit of an associate company, unless the

           In its 1996 Merger Policy Statement, the Commission explained that the statutory

“consistent with the public interest” standard gives the Commission “broad authority in

determining what is in the public interest,” and while the statute contains no presumption

disfavoring or favoring proposed mergers, “[i]t is applicants’ responsibility to

demonstrate that the merger is consistent with the public interest.”19

II.         Discussion

            A.      The Commission should condition any authorization of the proposed
                    merger on the removal of the RTO Adder from VEPCO’s
                    transmission formula rate.

            Under its Merger Policy Statement, the Commission generally takes account of

three factors when analyzing a proposed merger: “the effect on competition, the effect on

rates, and the effect on regulation.”31 With respect to the effect on rates, the Merger

 Policy Statement declares that “in order to ensure that a merger is consistent with the

public interest,” the Commission “must protect the merging utilities’ wholesale

ratepayers and transmission customers from the possible adverse effects of the merger.”32

        That principle is particularly important here. Applicants contend that the proposed

merger will position the combined company to undertake substantial future transmission

investment in the Dominion Zone and profit from significant large-load and infrastructure

growth opportunities. As those investments are incorporated into transmission rates,

customers should not be required to continue paying for incentive rate treatment that no

longer serves its intended purpose.33

        VEPCO currently enjoys a higher return on its transmission rate base through

inclusion of an “RTO Adder” on top of its authorized base return on equity (“ROE”),

even though VEPCO’s RTO participation is required by Virginia law and no longer

reflects the type of voluntary conduct that the Commission sought to encourage through

incentive rate treatment. While VEPCO’s RTO Adder no longer induces the conduct it

was designed to promote, it continues to increase transmission rates paid by customers. In

evaluating the rate effects of the proposed merger, the Commission should not permit the

combined company to continue recovering an incentive that no longer satisfies its

underlying rationale. Accordingly, the Commission should condition any approval of the

proposed transaction on elimination of VEPCO’s RTO Adder.

            In its 2008 order accepting VEPCO’s proposed transmission formula rate, the

Commission granted VEPCO’s request for the RTO Adder in its transmission formula

           But the Commission’s 2008 order is no longer good law. In that Commission

proceeding, the Virginia State Corporation Commission Staff and North Carolina

Agencies opposed VEPCO’s request for the RTO Adder on the grounds that the Virginia

that awarding the RTO Adder to VEPCO was consistent with section 219 of the FPA38

and Order No. 679 notwithstanding the Virginia statute requiring VEPCO’s RTO

membership.39

automatically allocates fifty percent of net secondary-use revenues to shareholders

without regard to the relative contributions of customers and shareholders in creating

those revenues, the proposed merger increases the potential transfer of value from

customer-funded assets to shareholders. The resulting risk is particularly acute where

revenues are derived from passive uses of transmission facilities. The category-specific

revenue-credit condition proposed above is therefore necessary to ensure that merger-

enhanced opportunities to monetize transmission facilities benefit customers in a manner

commensurate with their investment in those assets and to help ensure that the proposed

merger is consistent with the public interest.


III.   Conclusion

       The Commission should authorize the Applicants’ proposed merger only under

the conditions set forth above.
